zh.q: 煤挖出来直接烧不是挺好吗，为什么要先变成气？
zh.concl: 煤是碳为主的复杂混合物，直接烧只拿到热，硫、尘、氮跟着排；气化把碳变成 CO + H₂ 组成的可调气，才能当合成氨、甲醇的原料。
points: 煤主要含碳，另有氢、氧、氮、硫（烟煤约 C 84.4 %、S 1.8 %）。
直接燃烧：只拿到热，SO₂、粉尘、NOₓ 一起排出去。
气化：用蒸汽与氧气把碳变成 CO + H₂，成为组成可调的化工原料气。

zh.q: 气化是吸热的，热量从哪来？为什么非要同时通氧和水蒸气？
zh.concl: C + H₂O(g) → CO + H₂ 要吸 131.3 kJ·mol⁻¹，这部分热只能靠烧掉一部分煤。氧气多则炉温高、转化率高，但有效气被 CO₂ 稀释——氧气管供热，蒸汽管产氢。
points: 气化主式要吸 131.3 kJ·mol⁻¹，热量只能靠烧掉一部分煤。
供热靠部分燃烧：C + O₂ → CO₂ 放 393.5 kJ·mol⁻¹；2C + O₂ → 2CO 放 221.1 kJ·mol⁻¹。
氧煤比 0.26 → 0.30：炉温 +106 ℃、碳转化率 +4.8 个百分点、有效气 −1.0 个百分点。

zh.q: 一千多度的炉子里，煤到底经历了什么？灰又去哪了？
zh.concl: 煤浆与氧气并流喷入：先烧（约 1600 ℃）、再气化（约 1400 ℃），出气在激冷段降到 300 ℃ 以下，熔渣落进渣池。温度必须高于灰熔点，灰才能以液态渣排走。
points: 煤浆与氧气从顶置烧嘴并流喷入，先剧烈燃烧（约 1600 ℃），再被水蒸气气化（约 1400 ℃）。
出气在激冷段被水直接冷却到 300 ℃ 以下，才能去洗涤与变换。
气流床温度远高于灰熔点，灰以液态熔渣从渣口排出；几乎没有焦油，甲烷只有百分之一二。

zh.q: 多通点水蒸气不是能多产氢吗？为什么不能一直加？
zh.concl: 蒸汽多 → 吸热多、炉温低 → H₂/CO 升高，但温度掉下来碳转化率跟着掉；蒸汽少 → 温度高、H₂/CO 偏低。蒸汽与氧气是一对跷跷板，参考工况 0.26 / 0.55 就是它们的折中。
points: 水蒸气两个作用同向不同价：多产氢，但吃掉炉温。

zh.q: 气化气里 H₂ 和 CO 的比例是固定的，下游要的比例不一样怎么办？
zh.concl: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂ 是放热可逆反应：温度低，平衡对 CO 的转化更彻底；温度高，出口 CO 剩得多。煤气化用耐硫变换（Co-Mo），带着 H₂S 也能干活。变换是调比例的工段，不是越多越好。
points: 变换 ΔH = −41.2 kJ·mol⁻¹（由 NIST 生成焓相减，与维基转引一致）。

zh.q: 气里那点硫黄味儿的东西，为什么非除掉不可？
zh.concl: 煤里的硫在炉内变成 H₂S，耐硫变换又把 COS 转成 H₂S。它进甲醇合成塔（铜基）或氨合成塔（铁基）会让催化剂中毒失活，排出去就是 SO₂。所以用 −40 ℃ 的甲醇一次把 H₂S 与 CO₂ 吸掉，硫送克劳斯变成硫磺。
points: 煤中硫 0.2–5 %（烟煤约 1.8 %），气化后主要是 H₂S，耐硫变换把 COS 也转成 H₂S。
低温甲醇洗：−40 ℃ 甲醇、2.76–6.89 MPa，可分别回收 H₂S 与 CO₂。
克劳斯：2H₂S + O₂ → 2S + 2H₂O，热反应段 >850 ℃，受平衡限制要多段。

zh.q: 同样是这套气，怎么一会儿做甲醇、一会儿做合成氨？
zh.concl: 甲醇要 H₂/CO ≈ 2，合成氨要 H₂/N₂ = 3。甲醇走部分变换 + 旁路配气（55 % 过变换炉）；合成氨走深度变换 + 配氮（氮来自空分）。同一个气化岛，改的是变换深度与配气配氮。
points: 甲醇合成每 mol CO 耗 2 mol H₂（CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH），CO₂ 也参与。
合成氨 3H₂ + N₂ ⇌ 2NH₃，配比 3 : 1，氮来自空分。
本课设定：甲醇路线 φ = 0.55（旁路配气）；合成氨路线 φ = 1.00（全变换），200 ℃ 时出口 CO 1.16 %。

zh.q: 考核：你来当班长——能不能把气调成甲醇要的比例，又不把炉子烧坏？
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：氧煤比定温度与纯度，蒸汽煤比定氢与温度，变换温度定比例，脱硫定合成催化剂能不能活。四个旋钮各管一头，凑在一起才是合格的原料气。
points: 三个滑杆都要在操作带内：氧煤比 0.23–0.30、蒸汽煤比 0.40–0.70、变换 200–450 ℃。
炉温 ≥ 1550 ℃（氧煤比推太高）走「3 秒倒计时 → 超温 → 复盘」；≤ 1200 ℃（蒸汽推太多）走低温链。

en.q: Isn't it fine to just burn coal as mined? Why turn it into gas first?
en.concl: Coal is a complex carbon-rich mixture; burning it gives only heat, with sulfur, dust and nitrogen emitted. Gasification turns the carbon into an adjustable CO + H₂ gas that can feed ammonia and methanol synthesis.
points: Coal is mostly carbon, plus hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur (bituminous coal about C 84.4 %, S 1.8 %).
Direct burning gives only heat, releasing SO₂, dust and NOₓ along with it.
Gasification uses steam and oxygen to turn carbon into CO + H₂, a chemical feed gas of adjustable composition.

en.q: Gasification is endothermic. Where does the heat come from? Why feed oxygen and steam together?
en.concl: C + H₂O(g) → CO + H₂ absorbs 131.3 kJ·mol⁻¹, and that heat can only come from burning part of the coal. More oxygen means higher temperature and conversion, but useful gas is diluted by CO₂: the oxygen line supplies heat, the steam line supplies hydrogen.
points: The main gasification reaction absorbs 131.3 kJ·mol⁻¹, and the heat can only come from burning part of the coal.
Heat comes from partial combustion: C + O₂ → CO₂ releases 393.5 kJ·mol⁻¹; 2C + O₂ → 2CO releases 221.1 kJ·mol⁻¹.
Oxygen-to-coal ratio 0.26 → 0.30: temperature +106 ℃, carbon conversion +4.8 points, useful gas −1.0 point.

en.q: In a gasifier at over a thousand degrees, what does the coal go through? Where does the ash go?
en.concl: Coal slurry and oxygen enter co-currently: burning first (about 1600 ℃), then gasification (about 1400 ℃); the outlet gas drops below 300 ℃ in the quench section and molten slag falls into the slag bath. The temperature must be above the ash melting point so ash can leave as liquid slag.
points: Coal slurry and oxygen are sprayed in co-currently from the top burner, first burning fiercely (about 1600 ℃), then gasified by steam (about 1400 ℃).
The outlet gas is cooled directly with water in the quench section to below 300 ℃ before going to scrubbing and shift.
An entrained-flow bed runs far above the ash melting point, so ash leaves as liquid slag through the slag outlet; there is almost no tar and only one or two percent methane.

en.q: Doesn't more steam give more hydrogen? Why not keep adding it?
en.concl: More steam → more heat absorbed, lower temperature → H₂/CO rises, but carbon conversion falls with the temperature; less steam → higher temperature, H₂/CO too low. Steam and oxygen are a seesaw, and the reference 0.26 / 0.55 is their compromise.
points: Steam-to-coal ratio 0.55 → 0.70: temperature −85 ℃, H₂/CO 2.33 → 2.61, carbon conversion −6.3 points.
H₂ rises from 33.5 % to 37.5 % and CO falls from 46.0 % to 42.0 % (dry basis).
Steam's two effects come together at different prices: more hydrogen, but it eats the temperature.

en.q: The H₂ to CO ratio in gasifier gas is fixed. What if downstream needs a different ratio?
en.concl: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂ is exothermic and reversible: at low temperature equilibrium converts CO more completely; at high temperature more CO remains at the outlet. Coal gasification uses sour shift (Co-Mo), which works with H₂S present. Shift is the unit that adjusts the ratio, and more is not always better.
points: Shift ΔH = −41.2 kJ·mol⁻¹ (from NIST enthalpies of formation, matching the figure quoted on Wikipedia).

en.q: Why must that little bit of rotten-egg-smelling stuff in the gas be removed?
en.concl: Sulfur in coal becomes H₂S in the gasifier, and sour shift turns COS into H₂S as well. Entering a methanol (copper-based) or ammonia (iron-based) reactor it poisons and deactivates the catalyst, and released it becomes SO₂. So methanol at −40 ℃ absorbs H₂S and CO₂ in one go, and the sulfur goes to Claus to become elemental sulfur.
points: Coal contains 0.2–5 % sulfur (bituminous about 1.8 %); after gasification it is mainly H₂S, and sour shift converts COS to H₂S too.
Rectisol: methanol at −40 ℃ and 2.76–6.89 MPa can recover H₂S and CO₂ separately.
Claus: 2H₂S + O₂ → 2S + 2H₂O, thermal stage >850 ℃, limited by equilibrium so several stages are needed.

en.q: With the same gas, how can we make methanol one moment and ammonia the next?
en.concl: Methanol needs H₂/CO ≈ 2, ammonia needs H₂/N₂ = 3. Methanol uses partial shift + bypass blending (55 % through the shift reactor); ammonia uses deep shift + added nitrogen (from air separation). Same gasification island; what changes is the shift depth and the blending or nitrogen.
points: Methanol synthesis uses 2 mol H₂ per mol CO (CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH), and CO₂ also takes part.
Ammonia synthesis 3H₂ + N₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ needs a 3 : 1 ratio, with nitrogen from air separation.
Lesson setting: methanol route φ = 0.55 (bypass blending); ammonia route φ = 1.00 (full shift), outlet CO 1.16 % at 200 ℃.

en.q: Check: you are the shift leader. Can you bring the gas to the ratio methanol needs without wrecking the gasifier?
en.concl: The check has no new conclusion: the oxygen-to-coal ratio sets temperature and purity, the steam-to-coal ratio sets hydrogen and temperature, shift temperature sets the ratio, and desulfurization decides whether the synthesis catalyst survives. Four knobs, each with its own job, together make a qualified feed gas.
points: All three sliders must stay in their operating bands: oxygen-to-coal 0.23–0.30, steam-to-coal 0.40–0.70, shift 200–450 ℃.
Gasifier ≥ 1550 ℃ (oxygen too high) leads to "3 s countdown → overtemperature → review"; ≤ 1200 ℃ (too much steam) leads to the low-temperature chain.
H₂/CO is adjusted with shift temperature: 2.01 at 400 ℃, 2.33 at 320 ℃.
